title: Many Judaisms
hook: Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes and others argue over law and Temple

segments.voice: Yesterday, King Yannai wore two crowns, and a sage told him one should be enough. Your line was heroes can change. How did you use your bit of power? Today, the arguments in Jerusalem multiply. Day eight hundred ninety-five.

One man in Jerusalem wants to find the right way to live, so he tries all of them. That's how the historian Josephus describes his own youth. There were, he says, three schools of thought among the Jews: the Pharisees, the Sadducees and the Essenes. He went through all three, the hard way, from the inside. Then, still not satisfied, he went out to the desert and lived with a teacher named Bannus, who wore clothes made from what grew on trees, ate only what grew wild, and bathed in cold water day and night. Only after all that did he come back to the city and choose. His search tells us something on its own: in those days, being Jewish came in more than one shape.
screen: `A YOUNG MAN TRIES ALL THREE.` → `A TEACHER IN THE DESERT.` → `MORE THAN ONE SHAPE.`

segments.voice: Here's how Josephus lays out the schools. The Pharisees keep many customs handed down from the fathers that are not written in the law of Moses, and they teach that souls live on after death. The Sadducees hold that only the written laws are binding, and say the soul does not outlive the body; Josephus says they were fewer in number but included people of high rank. The Essenes live in close communities and share their property in common, so that no one is rich and no one is poor among them. And Josephus adds a fourth group, followers of Judas the Galilean, who say God alone is their ruler and will call no man master. The Mishnah, the rabbis' own book, lets us hear two of these groups argue. In tractate Yadayim, the Sadducees complain to the Pharisees: you say holy scriptures make the hands impure, but the books the Mishnah calls Hamiram don't? Some readers take that word to mean Homer. Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai answers, and the debate goes on, round after round, each side making its case. Notice the shape. These aren't people who've lost their faith. They're people who care so much about the Torah and the Temple that they argue about every detail: what counts as Torah, who should run the Temple, what happens after death, how to live. In those days, there were many ways to be Jewish, and the Mishnah keeps the Sadducees' complaint in their own words.
screen: `PHARISEES: CUSTOMS FROM THE FATHERS.` · `SADDUCEES: ONLY WHAT'S WRITTEN.` · `ESSENES: EVERYTHING SHARED.` · then, large: `SADDUCEES AND PHARISEES ARGUE.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: respect a group unlike yours. Settle and breathe. Bring to mind a group whose way is different from yours: another congregation, another denomination, another political party, a family down the street that keeps its customs differently, or no customs at all. Picture one actual person from that group, someone with a face and a name. Then ask: what do they care about so much that they'd argue for it? Find one thing in them you can honestly respect. You don't have to agree. Just let the respect be real. If you pray, you can use words from your tradition to wish them well. The bell holds the time.
Many Judaisms. Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes and others, all arguing over Torah and Temple in the same land at the same time. Today's word.
Your line: many ways then too. Today, when you meet someone who does your tradition, or any tradition, differently, ask one curious question before you decide anything. Day eight hundred ninety-five.

howItsDone: Jews today belong to different movements and communities, such as Orthodox, Conservative, Reform and others, and study the Second Temple sects through the Mishnah, the Talmud and the writings of Josephus.

fork.setup: you're young Josephus in Jerusalem, wanting to find the right way to live. there are three schools. what do you do?
options: pick the biggest one and stop asking.
go through all three, then live with a teacher in the desert.
decide none of them matter and walk away.
fork.reveal: Josephus says he went through all three schools, then lived with Bannus in the desert, and only then came back to the city and chose.

original.note: Hebrew: Perushim, the Mishnah's name for the Pharisees, as in tractate Yadayim.

trapdoor: what you thought: ancient Judaism was one uniform religion.
what it means: Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes and others argued over Torah, Temple and the afterlife in the same city.
what a scholar hears: Josephus describes the schools in Antiquities 18 and Jewish War 2, and his own search in his Life; Mishnah Yadayim 4:6–8 records Sadducees and Pharisees debating.

notes: Josephus paraphrased throughout (Whiston is not on the public-domain list here). Life 2 gives his age (sixteen) and three years with Bannus; the script omits the numbers. Please confirm the Bannus details (clothing from trees, wild food, cold bathing day and night).

Josephus on the Pharisees' unwritten customs is Antiquities 13.10.6; on the soul, Antiquities 18.1.3–4 and War 2.8.14; Sadducees 'few but of high rank' Antiquities 18.1.4; Essenes' common property War 2.8.3; the fourth philosophy Antiquities 18.1.6. Please confirm the summaries are fair to each group.
